Choosing the right answer from a medical
VLM's own samples

PART I

The field's vocabulary

Every term used later, defined once, with the name the literature uses.

I · Vocabulary

Medical visual question answering: two answer formats

SLAKE, abdominal CT (question 12231).
Closed-endedanswer from a fixed set: yes/no, or a letter among options (multiple choice). Grading is trivial: string equality. “Is the liver visible?” → yes
Open-ended (free text) — this workthe model writes the answer. Many correct strings exist (“large bowel”, “colon”, “large intestine”), so grading needs either exact match after normalisation or a grader model (LLM-as-a-judge). “What organ is the gray part on the left of the image?” → gold: Large Bowel
Why open-endedit is what a clinician-facing system faces, and it is where selection signals work: in this project, error detection reached AUROC ≈ 0.87 on free text vs ≈ 0.6 on 4-option multiple choice.
AUROC figures: project finding 2 (PROJECT_RETROSPECTIVE_2026-07-29.md §5.2), from the earlier multiple-choice phase

I · Vocabulary

How a VLM answers: Lingshu-7B (Qwen2.5-VL-7B architecture)

vision encoder (ViT)turns image patches into vectors (window attention)
merger / projectormaps them to the language model's width — each becomes an image token
decoder (LLM)reads system + image + question tokens, writes the answer one token at a time
hidden statethe 3,584-number vector at one position after one block (the residual stream)
Qwen2.5-VL report Table 1 p.4, §2.1 p.3–5; Lingshu §3 p.9 (built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct); token bound derived (14-px patches, 2×2 merge)
6
I · Vocabulary

Decoding: greedy vs sampling, and what temperature does

greedy decodingalways take the most likely next token. One answer, deterministic. Our baseline.
temperature samplingdraw the next token at random from $$p_i=\frac{e^{u_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{u_j/T}}$$ \(u_i\) = the model's logit for token i. T → 0 is greedy; larger T spreads probability, so repeated samples differ. Ours: plain temperature sampling, T = 0.7, max 64 tokens; no top-p / top-k set (run_openvqa.py).
not to be confused withtemperature scaling, a calibration method that rescales a classifier's logits after training. Unrelated.
distinct answers among 8 samples (macro mean)
oracle@8 — at least one of the 8 is correct (judge, macro)
Both y-axes are truncated (they do not start at 0).
head_temp_ensemble_2026-08-30.json — cells.*.{T}.mean_distinct and .oracle, macro over 8 benchmarks, held-out image halves, N = 8
7
I · Vocabulary

Best-of-N: coverage and selection are two different problems

best-of-Nsample N answers, return one chosen by a scoring rule (a.k.a. repeated sampling, n-best reranking).
oracle@N = pass@N = coverageshare of questions with ≥ 1 correct answer among the N — the ceiling for any selector.
selectionfinding it without the gold. Brown: precision; Bay: the identifiability gap.
selection efficiency (ours)selected ÷ oracle@N per benchmark, then averaged: 0.81 (ratio of the two macro bars: 0.85). Not a standard name.
final_eval_FINAL_cap320_T07.json — cells.*.all.{greedy,pick,oracle}_judge, macro; selection efficiency per benchmark: numbers_review_part1.json (derived from final_eval_FINAL_cap320_T07.json by review/scr/w1_micro.py); Brown et al. 2024 p.2; Bay & Yearick 2026 abstract

I · Vocabulary

What a probe is — and what it does not prove

probesmall classifier on a frozen network's internal vectorsAlain & Bengio 2016; Q-Probe §2
linear probe\( \sigma(w^\top h + b) \) — the diagnostic standard
MLP probe (ours)\( w_2^\top\,\mathrm{GELU}(W_1 h + b_1) + b_2 \) — one hidden layer, width 256
correctness is decodable — an old findingAzaria & Mitchell · CCS · Kadavath: one statement each, not N answers
decodable ≠ causalreadable from the vector ≠ used by the model (Belinkov 2022)
control task & selectivityreal accuracy − accuracy on random labels (Hewitt & Liang 2019) not yet run for our probe — on the limits slide
transfer“error detectors fail to generalize across datasets” (Orgad 2024)
our use is operationalwe judge the probe only by the accuracy of the answers it chooses
Q-Probe arXiv:2402.14688 §2 p.2; Alain & Bengio arXiv:1610.01644; Hewitt & Liang EMNLP 2019; Belinkov, Computational Linguistics 48(1) 2022; Azaria & Mitchell arXiv:2304.13734; Burns et al. arXiv:2212.03827 (ICLR 2023); Kadavath et al. arXiv:2207.05221; Orgad et al. arXiv:2410.02707 (abstracts, via guide cards)

I · Vocabulary

Related but different: uncertainty estimation is not selection

confidence / uncertainty estimationbest-of-N selection (ours)
question asked“is this answer (or question) likely wrong?”“which of the N answers to this question is right?”
unit scoredone answer, or the question itselfevery candidate of one question
what mattersranking across questions (AUROC) and calibration (ECE)ranking within one question only
examplessemantic entropy (Farquhar, Nature 2024), semantic-entropy probes (SEPs, Kossen 2024), verbalised confidence; P(True) is per answer, so it can rank — that is the self-verification selectorverifiers, reward models, our probe
semantic entropy cannot pickit is one number per question, identical for all 8 candidates. Its only per-candidate quantity is cluster size — a majority vote by meaning.
calibration cannot reorderPlatt / temperature scaling are monotone: they change the numbers, never which candidate is first (Byun et al. 2026, Table 2).
shared mechanismhidden-state probes appear on both sides; ours is the per-candidate correctness variant used as a within-question ranker.
Farquhar et al. Nature 630 (2024) Eq. 3 p.8; Kossen et al. arXiv:2406.15927; Byun et al. arXiv:2604.02543 Table 2 p.7; Geng et al. NAACL 2024

II · Key papers

The idea is old: rerank a generator's candidates with a trained scorer

Collins & Koo, Comp. Ling. 31(1) 2005; Li et al. arXiv:2010.11428 (CEM), 2103.14152 (R-EBM); Cobbe arXiv:2110.14168; Nakano arXiv:2112.09332; Jumper, Nature 2021; arXiv:2402.14688, 2505.12225 (SWIFT, KDD 2026), 2504.16760, 2608.30841, 2608.17124, 2605.28527 (VLA probe), 2609.04336, 2609.06419

II · Key papers

Trained verifiers: Cobbe et al. 2021 (OpenAI)

Figure 4 from Cobbe et al. 2021 (p.7): the verifier training pipeline, shown for illustration
domain
text · grade-school math word problems (numeric answers)
models
GPT-3 6B and 175B generators, fine-tuned; verifier = a same-size LM, full fine-tune
benchmarks
GSM8K (introduced here: 7.5K train / 1K test)
for us
our recipe: outcome labels → trained scorer → argmax, with a 918k-parameter probe as the verifier
method, step by step
  1. fine-tune a GPT-3 generator on GSM8K for 2 epochs (a calculator evaluates <<…>> annotations)
  2. sample 100 solutions per training problem; label each correct / incorrect by its final answer only
  3. train a verifier: a same-size LM initialised from the generator, a scalar head on a special token; MSE loss (+ the language-modelling loss), 1 epoch; default = a value after every token (token-level)
  4. at test time sample 100 solutions at T = 0.7 and return the highest-scored one
Cobbe et al. arXiv:2110.14168: Fig. 4 p.7; §4.2 p.8, §4.3 p.9, §5.1 p.10, §6 p.12, Table 1 p.16 (PAPER_NOTES_A §1.1); Gao et al. arXiv:2210.10760

II · Key papers

Coverage vs precision: Brown et al. 2024 (Large Language Monkeys)

Figure 1 from Brown et al. 2024 (p.2): repeated sampling, then a verifier, shown for illustration
domain
text · math, formal proofs (Lean4), code
models
Llama-3 8B / 8B-Instruct / 70B-Instruct, Gemma 2B / 7B, Pythia, DeepSeek-Coder-V2; nothing trained
benchmarks
GSM8K, MATH, MiniF2F-MATH, CodeContests, SWE-bench Lite
for us
coverage = our oracle@8; selection is what the probe does
method, step by step
  1. take an existing model — nothing is trained
  2. sample k answers per problem at a fixed temperature (MATH / GSM8K 0.6, MiniF2F 0.5, CodeContests 0.6 with top-p 0.95, SWE-bench 1.6), k up to 10,000
  3. coverage = share of problems solved by any sample (unbiased pass@k estimator)
  4. where an automatic checker exists (unit tests, Lean proof checker) it picks the answer; on GSM8K / MATH compare majority vote, a reward model (ArmoRM-Llama3-8B) and reward-weighted vote
  5. fit coverage vs k with an exponentiated power law; compare models at equal FLOPs
Brown et al. arXiv:2407.21787: Fig. 1 p.2; §2–4, p.3, Fig. 7 p.10 (PAPER_NOTES_A §1.2)

II · Key papers

Test-time compute vs model size: Snell et al. 2024

Figure 2 from Snell et al. 2024 (p.8): three ways to search against a verifier, shown for illustration
domain
text · competition math
models
PaLM 2-S* base; verifier = a process reward model (PRM), PaLM 2-S* fine-tuned; a revision model
benchmarks
MATH (Lightman et al. split, 500 test problems)
method, step by step
  1. proposer: PaLM 2-S*, plus a fine-tuned revision model that rewrites its own answer
  2. verifier: a process reward model (PRM) — PaLM 2-S* fine-tuned with BCE on per-step correctness estimated by Monte-Carlo rollouts
  3. search against the verifier: best-of-N weighted (sum scores over identical answers), beam search or lookahead; budgets up to 256 generations
  4. estimate each question's difficulty (5 bins, from 2,048 samples or the PRM score) and choose the best strategy per bin by two-fold cross-validation — “compute-optimal”
  5. compare with a ~14× larger model at equal FLOPs
Snell et al. arXiv:2408.03314 (ICLR 2025): Fig. 2 p.8, abstract, Fig. 4 p.10, Fig. 9 p.15, App. D p.22, App. F p.24–25 (PAPER_NOTES_A §1.3); ours: final_eval_FINAL_cap320_T07.json cells.{omnimed_open,vqamed_open}

Majority vote: self-consistency (Wang et al. 2023)

Figure 1 from Wang et al. 2023 (p.2): greedy chain of thought vs sampled paths and a vote, shown for illustration
domain
text · arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning (chain of thought)
models
UL2-20B, GPT-3 (code-davinci-001/002), LaMDA-137B, PaLM-540B; few-shot, nothing trained
benchmarks
GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA, AddSub, MultiArith, ASDiv, CSQA, StrategyQA, ARC
for us
the standard training-free baseline; on our open answers it loses to greedy (voting chart, a few slides on)
method, step by step
  1. few-shot chain-of-thought prompt; nothing is trained
  2. sample m = 40 reasoning paths (T = 0.5–0.7; PaLM: T = 0.7, top-k 40)
  3. parse each path's final answer
  4. return the most frequent answer (majority vote); weighted variants use the path's length-normalised probability

Training-free selection and its ceiling: majority vote, USC, embeddings

Wang et al. ICLR 2023

Self-consistency = majority vote

\( \hat a = \arg\max_a \sum_i \mathbb 1[a_i=a] \) · GSM8K 56.5 → 74.4 · needs exact repeats
Bay & Yearick 2026 · arXiv:2606.28661

The modal ceiling

voting is capped at \( \pi_{mode}=P[\text{mode is correct}] \), whatever N

For free text

consistency by LLM, embedding cluster, or own logits — none run on our pools

II · Key papers

The first probe reranker: Q-Probe (Li et al., ICML 2024)

Figure 1 from Li et al. 2024 (p.2): one feature vector per sampled program, scored by a probe, shown for illustration
domain
text · code generation (also grade-school math, human preferences)
models
Code-LLaMA-7B, frozen; probe = linear, 4,096 weights, on layer 26's embedding of prompt + completion
benchmarks
MBPP, HumanEval, GSM8K; HH / OASST / SHP preferences (GPT-4 win rate)
method, step by step
  1. sample k = 48 programs from frozen Code-LLaMA-7B (T = 0.8, top-p 0.95)
  2. embed prompt + completion with layer 26 of the same model
  3. score each with a linear probe (4,096 weights + bias)
  4. train on unit-test success with MSE, cross-entropy or a within-prompt policy-gradient loss (Adam, lr 5e-5, 150 epochs)
  5. pick by sampling from softmax(score / β); β → 0 is the argmax (best-of-k)

Rewards from hidden states: SWIFT (Guo et al., KDD 2026)

Figure 1 from Guo et al. 2026 (p.2): a large reward model vs SWIFT's linear head on all layers, shown for illustration
domain
text · math, code, commonsense, symbolic reasoning, safety
models
Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Ministral-8B, frozen; head = linear gate + linear token reward, 1.8–3.0×10⁵ parameters
benchmarks
MATH, GSM8K, AQuA_RAT, Imbue Code, HellaSwag, CoinFlip, PKU-SafeRLHF
method, step by step
  1. sample N paths per problem (T = 1.0, top-p 0.9, ≤ 1,024 tokens; N = 4–64)
  2. at every answer token, concatenate the hidden states of all layers (L × d numbers)
  3. one linear map → a token reward rt and a gate gt = σ(·)
  4. answer reward R = Σ gtrt / Σ gt (gate-weighted mean over tokens)
  5. train with BCE on answer correctness (6,000 problems × 8 paths, AdamW, early stopping); pick argmax R

A small reader on hidden states: HSRM (Li & Zhu 2026)

Figure 1 from Li & Zhu 2026 (p.3): hidden states at reasoning-step boundaries feed a 2M-parameter reader, shown for illustration
domain

models
Qwen3 1.7B–14B and Llama-3 1B–8B generators, frozen; reader = 2-layer Transformer → mean → linear, 2.1–3.4 M parameters

method, step by step
  1. sample candidates from a frozen generator (T = 0.7, top-p 0.9; train pools N = 64, evaluation N = 8)
  2. take final-layer hidden states at reasoning-step boundaries (the token before each line break, ≤ 100 steps)
  3. reader: linear projection → 2-layer Transformer (d = 256, 4 heads) → mean → LayerNorm → linear score; 2.1–3.4 M parameters
  4. train on cached states with a pairwise Bradley–Terry loss within each problem (all-right / all-wrong problems dropped); AdamW, lr 1e-4, 1,000 steps
  5. return the highest-scored candidate; labels from a symbolic checker plus an LLM judge on unresolved cases

When hidden-state selection beats voting: CASE (Wang, Hong, Bagci 2026)

Figure 1 from Wang, Hong & Bagci 2026 (p.8): voting vs CASE on the same 5 candidates, shown for illustration
domain
text · multiple-choice and short-answer QA: logic, medicine, math
models
12 LLMs incl. Qwen2.5 1.5–14B, Llama-3-8B, OpenBioLLM-8B/70B, Med42-8B; gate = logistic regression on the answer-token state
benchmarks
LogiQA, MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, MATH-500, GSM8K, GPQA
method, step by step
  1. sample 16–20 candidates per question (τ = 0.7, top-p 0.95)
  2. read the residual-stream state at the answer token (option letter or final answer token), one teacher-forced pass
  3. gate = standardise + ℓ2 logistic regression (C = 1.0), 5-fold cross-validation grouped by question
  4. operating layer: the late layer with the best within-question AUC
  5. pick the candidate with the highest gate score; compare with majority vote

II · Key papers

Teacher-forced replay for confidence: DualRead (Xie et al. 2026)

Figure 2 from Xie et al. 2026 (p.3): replaying the answer, reading states before and after it, shown for illustration
domain
vision-language · medical VQA, confidence of one answer
models
GRPO-trained Qwen3-VL-2B and MedGemma1.5-4B, frozen; small MLP / linear readers on final-layer states
benchmarks
SLAKE-test (in-distribution); VQA-RAD, PathVQA, PMC-VQA, OmniMedVQA, ReXVQA, VQA-Med 2019 (out of distribution)
for us
the same teacher-forced re-read as ours; its drop on new datasets is a warning about transfer
method, step by step
  1. train an actor VLM with GRPO on SLAKE-train (group size 8), then freeze it
  2. replay its greedy answer with teacher forcing
  3. read final-layer states: the last prompt token (MLP 256 → 128, class-weighted BCE) and the closing answer token (linear head); a visual branch uses the answer-token mean to pool image-token states
  4. temperature-scale each branch and average their log-odds into one confidence
  5. readers fit on image-disjoint partitions of SLAKE-train

II · Key papers

A published medical selector: WED (Hagen et al. 2026)

Figure 1 from Hagen et al. 2026 (p.3): generator and verifier rankings converge; the Wasserstein rule stops earlier, shown for illustration
domain
vision-language · open-ended medical VQA
models
Qwen3-VL-2B / 4B / 8B, Gemma-3-4B, MedGemma-4B; nothing trained — the same VLM plays generator and verifier
benchmarks
VQA-RAD and PathVQA open-ended test subsets, yes/no excluded; graded by Grok 4.1 Fast, EM, F1
for us
evaluated on two of our open benchmarks → we ran its code on our candidates (Part VI)
method, step by step
  1. sample until 8 distinct candidates or 16 draws (T ∈ {0.5, 1.0}); strip filler; merge synonyms (SapBERT)
  2. score each candidate with the same VLM, teacher-forced: as generator (likelihood under a “correct” vs “incorrect” framing) and as verifier (P(correct | image, question, candidate))
  3. generator and verifier update toward each other with no-regret steps (λ = η = 0.4) — arithmetic on small tables, no further VLM calls
  4. stop when the Wasserstein-1 distance between their distributions (SapBERT distances) is below δ = 0.2
  5. return the generator's top candidate under the “correct” signal (authors' code)

Claim-level checking: Best-of-Evidence (Zhang et al. 2026)

Figure 1 from Zhang et al. 2026 (p.1): a fixed candidate pool, a claim graph, budgeted evidence checks, shown for illustration
domain
vision-language · medical VQA (open and multiple choice)
models
generator Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B (16 samples, T = 1.1); evidence judge Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B
benchmarks

its baseline is voting, not greedy — the matching number for us is probe − vote (Part VI)
method, step by step

  5. update each candidate's score with the evidence and return the maximum

III · Method

Which layers: 18, 20, 22 of 28 — upper-middle depth

indexing“layer ℓ” = hidden_states[ℓ] = residual stream after decoder block ℓ (index 0 = embeddings). Relative depth 0.64 / 0.71 / 0.79.
why three layerssingle layers 18–22 all give +0.101 to +0.104 (5 benchmarks); the 18/20/22 ensemble +0.105. The spread (≈ 0.003) is noise level, so three layers are a hedge against picking the wrong one, not a measured gain (pooled: +0.0007).
how chosenon image half A, 5 of 8 benchmarks, judge only, no interval. Half B is out of sample for this choice.
literatureHSRM: upper layers strongest, the final layer “not always the unique optimum”. MedProb: peak at layer 28 (MCQ task).

III · Method

Step 3 — the probe: one hidden layer, 918,017 parameters

$$\tilde h_i^{(\ell)}=\big(\bar h_i^{(\ell)}-\mu^{(\ell)}\big)\oslash\big(s^{(\ell)}+\epsilon\big)$$
$$f_{\ell,k}\big(\tilde h_i^{(\ell)}\big)=w_2^{\top}\,\mathrm{GELU}\!\left(W_1 \tilde h_i^{(\ell)}+b_1\right)+b_2$$
parametershapecount
\(W_1\)256 × 3584917,504
\(b_1\)256256
\(w_2\)256256
\(b_2\)11
total918,017
\(i\) = distinct answer, \(k\) = seed (0–7); \(\mu, s\): training-set mean / std per dimension (\(\epsilon=10^{-6}\)), frozen with the probe.
reads asa score, not a calibrated probability; only its order within a question is used.
ckpts/train/final_probe_2026-10-16/fold{0,1} (recipe.json: Linear(3584→256)-GELU-Linear(256→1)); 3584·256+256+256+1 = 918,017; standardiser: final_method_eval.py (std + 1e-6)
54
III · Method

Training the probe: labels, loss, data

label \(c_i\in\{0,1\}\)is answer \(y_i\) correct? — the training judge, MedVLThinker-32B (text-only, sees the gold); one label per (question, distinct answer)
loss: class-weighted binary cross-entropy$$\mathcal L=-\big[w_+\,c\log\sigma(f)+(1-c)\log(1-\sigma(f))\big]$$ \(w_+=(1-\pi)/\pi\approx3.8\); π = share of correct rows in the fold's training set (0.207 / 0.209). Uses every row, incl. all-right / all-wrong questions.
optimiserAdamW, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-2, 30 epochs (no early stopping), batch 256; 8 seeds × 3 layers = 24 probes per fold (a deep ensemble × a layer ensemble).
training rows115,934 / 116,000 per fold: other image half of the 8 open benchmarks + comparison sets + 4 extra sets: PathVQA/SLAKE/VQA-RAD train splits + Kvasir-VQA (breakdown: backup recipe)
what this meansthe probe learns the training judge's notion of correct; training needs labels per benchmark, inference needs no dataset label
final_eval_FINAL_cap320_T07.json folds.*.train_rows; head_sweep.py:172-174 (pos_weight = (1−π)/π); π and row breakdown: numbers_review_part2.json; final probes fitted on T = 0.7 pools
55
III · Method

Step 4 — the readout: rank averaging with a vote tie-break

$$\begin{aligned} r_i&=\frac1{24}\sum_{\ell,k}\frac{\operatorname{rank}_{\ell,k}(i)}{\max(n-1,1)}\\ \hat y&=\arg\max_i r_i\qquad(\text{ties}\to\arg\max_i v_i)\end{aligned}$$
n = distinct answers of this question (1 ≤ n ≤ N); rank = 0-based position in ascending score order, tied scores share the average rank (a Borda count). Ties in r → more votes; ties in votes too → first alphabetically.
why ranksthe 24 probes are trained independently; their raw scores are on different scales. Ranks are scale-free, and only the order within one question matters for an argmax. Averaging raw, standardised or calibrated scores tied (Part IV).
worked_example_12231.json (raw scores: candidates[*].probe_scores); readout: genframe_data.rank_avg (ties averaged, ÷ max(n−1, 1)), final_method_eval.py tie-break; adopted 2026-10-15 under a pre-specified rule (readout_variants_2026-10-15.json)

PART VI

Against published work

Three levels of comparability: same candidates · same metric code and test split · different protocol (context only).

79
VI · Comparison

How to compare honestly

tierwhat is held fixedcomparisonswhat may be claimed
1 · same candidatesimages, questions, the 8 samples, graders — only the selector differsWED (ran the authors' code on our pools)which selector is better on these candidates, with CIs
2 · same metric code / test splitthe official test questions and the scoring codeLLaVA-Med recall & closed accuracy; ImageCLEF VQA-Med 2019 testwhere our numbers sit — not a ranking (different generators, training data)
3 · different protocolnothingLingshu's published numbers; Best-of-Evidence; MedProb App. H; Verification Miragecontext only — never a ranking
why this mattersthe same Lingshu-7B scores 61.9 on PathVQA in its own paper (open: GPT-4.1 judge; closed: rule-scored) and 71.9 in an independent benchmark (step-by-step \boxed{} prompt, option-matched scoring, item set not stated): evaluation choices alone move the same model by ~10 points.

VII · Limits

Never tested — the honest gap list

selectors not run on our pools

  • log-probability ranking; probe + likelihood (rerankers since Collins 2005) — log-probs exist for the October 1-megapixel pools, 7 of 8 benchmarks
  • USC, embedding agreement (EBA), MBR, semantic-cluster vote
  • image-contrast scores (CEBaG, VASE)
  • a LoRA verifier trained on the same pooled data
  • WED with its own sampling loop (“as published”)

design axes not tested

  • ranking loss on the final recipe; learned (gated) pooling; LayerNorm in the probe; learning rate for BCE; number of seeds
  • per-question or per-modality temperature; adaptive N
  • temperature grid finer than 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.7 / 1.0; top-p, top-k with the probe

diagnostics not run

  • control task / selectivity (Hewitt & Liang)
  • within-question AUROC (CASE, HSRM)
  • image-shuffle control (MedProb)
  • probe-error vs generator-error coupling (Mirage)
  • human rating of the picks — none on the shipped method; no independent check at all on 5 of 8 benchmarks
  • variance over training resamples / image-split salt; template-clustered CIs
  • judge agreement on the final pools (κ = 0.79 is on September labels)
  • perceptual-hash near-duplicates resolved
